before.content_html:
Why Identifying Customers Comes First

Before a business designs a product, sets a price or books an advert, it has to answer one question: who is the customer and what do they want? Identifying customer needs is the starting point of all marketing. Get it wrong and everything else — price, packaging, shops, adverts — misses the target.

Gymshark is a useful UK example. Founder Ben Francis worked out that young gym-goers wanted sportswear that actually fitted muscular frames and looked good on Instagram. Identifying that specific need let Gymshark design the right products, charge premium prices and grow from a Birmingham garage to a billion-pound business in under a decade.

Key Fact

Businesses identify and satisfy customer needs to: (1) provide a product customers will actually buy, (2) increase sales, (3) select the correct marketing mix, (4) avoid costly mistakes, and (5) stay competitive against rivals.

The Cost of Getting It Wrong

Failing to understand customers is expensive. Research and development, manufacturing, packaging and launch adverts all cost money — and a product that nobody wants wastes every pound of it. Worse, the business may be stuck with unsold stock it has to sell at a loss. This is why identifying needs first reduces risk: the business commits cash only to products the market actually wants.

Meeting customer needs also feeds back into the marketing mix. Once you know who the customer is, you can decide what the product should look like, what price they will pay, where they shop, and which adverts they will actually see.

What Is Market Segmentation?

Market segmentation means splitting a whole market into smaller groups of customers who share similar characteristics. No business can please everyone, so it picks a segment, designs for that segment, and talks to that segment. The specification requires you to know four ways of segmenting: gender, age, location and income.

Gender — splitting the market by male, female or non-binary customers. Fragrance brands like Lynx design products almost entirely around young male shoppers, while Dove’s ‘Real Beauty’ campaigns target women. Gendered products, packaging and adverts can create a stronger emotional connection with one group.

Age — splitting the market into age bands. LEGO targets children aged 4–11, Netflix’s teen comedies target 13–19, and Saga holidays target the over-50s. Each age group has different spending power, different interests and different media habits.

Location — splitting the market by where customers live. A surf shop in Newquay stocks very different products to a ski shop in Aviemore, even though both are selling sports gear. Location affects weather, culture, language and what rivals are nearby.

Income — splitting the market by how much customers earn. Aldi and Lidl target shoppers who want the lowest price. Waitrose and Fortnum & Mason target higher-income households who will pay more for quality and service. Income segmentation shapes price, product quality and where the shops open.

Targeting a Segment in Practice

Zara, the Spanish fashion retailer, is built around segmenting by age, income and location. It targets fashion-conscious shoppers aged 18–35 on middle incomes who live in cities. Its shops are in high-footfall city centres like Oxford Street, its prices sit between Primark and designer brands, and its ‘fast fashion’ model refreshes stock every two weeks to chase the latest trends. Every element of the marketing mix flows from the segment decision — if Zara tried to target everyone from toddlers to pensioners it would please nobody.

Segmentation also opens up niche marketing. Instead of trying to be everything to everybody, a business picks one small group — like vegan-only cosmetics or plus-size sportswear — and dominates it. The segment may be small, but customers inside it are loyal because nobody else meets their specific needs. Lush, the UK cosmetics chain, built its reputation on one tight niche: hand-made, cruelty-free products sold in minimal packaging. That niche now sells in over 900 shops worldwide.

Most larger UK businesses use more than one segmentation base at the same time. Boots divides the health and beauty market by gender (men’s Boots range vs No7 for women), by age (Boots Baby vs Boots 50+ vitamins), by income (premium brands vs own-label) and by location (city-centre flagship stores, retail park ‘beauty’ stores, local pharmacies). Combining bases gives a much sharper picture of the customer than using one base alone — a 55-year-old woman on a high income shopping in central London has different needs to a 20-year-old man on a low income in a market town, even though both are Boots customers.

Key Fact

The four segmentation bases in the specification are gender, age, location and income. Each one lets a business design a marketing mix aimed at a specific group — rather than wasting money trying to please everyone.

Benefits: marketing spend is focused on people who are likely to buy, so the return on every pound is higher. Products are designed around real customer needs, which increases sales and customer loyalty. It also lets smaller firms compete with giants by owning a niche.

Drawbacks: segmentation can be expensive — the business needs market research to identify segments, and different segments may need different products, packaging and adverts. There is also a risk of stereotyping customers and missing buyers who do not fit the expected profile. A brand also needs to watch for segment drift over time — when Topshop stopped appealing to its core 16–25 segment, it collapsed into administration in 2021.

before.exam_tip_html: Examiners often give you a scenario and ask you to pick the ‘most appropriate’ pricing method. Do not just describe the method — link it to the specific business in the case study. For 9-mark ‘Justify’ answers, say why your chosen method beats at least one alternative in this scenario. Writing about USP and brand image from a real named business lifts you straight into the top band for 12-mark evaluations.

before.content_html:
Products Have a Life Cycle

Every product goes through stages over time — it is born, grows, peaks and eventually declines. The product life cycle (PLC) is the model businesses use to track this journey and decide what to do at each stage. Understanding it stops a business pumping money into a declining product or charging too little for one that is about to take off.

The Five Stages

Research & development (R&D) — the product is being designed and tested. Costs are high; revenue is zero. Dyson famously spent years developing the cyclone vacuum before the first one was sold.

Introduction — the product launches. Sales grow slowly as customers hear about it. Price may be set high (skimming) or low (penetration). Adverts are heavy. The business is often still making a loss on this product.

Growth — sales rise quickly as word spreads and rivals take notice. Profits turn positive as fixed development costs get spread over more units.

Maturity — sales peak and flatten. The market is saturated, competition is fierce, and prices may need to fall. The iPhone has been in maturity for several years — annual refreshes keep sales steady rather than booming.

Decline — sales fall as customers move to newer products. Nokia’s 2000s dominance in mobile phones collapsed into decline once Apple and Samsung launched smartphones.

Key Fact

The five stages of the product life cycle in order are: research & development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Drawing the PLC curve is not a tested exam skill — focus on interpreting what happens to sales and profit at each stage.

Extension Strategies

Extension strategies are how businesses push back the decline stage. The specification lists five: updating packaging, adding more or different features, changing the target market, advertising and price reduction. Cadbury’s Dairy Milk — in the UK market since 1905 — has survived through constant extension: Fruit & Nut, Whole Nut, Caramel, Oreo, Marvellous Creations, vegan plant-based versions, limited-edition flavours, new packaging designs. Each launch refreshes the brand.

Not every strategy suits every product. A simple price reduction may boost sales short-term but trains customers to expect cheaper prices. Adding features can backfire if the product becomes too complicated. Extension works best when it gives customers a genuine new reason to buy.

The Product Portfolio and the Boston Matrix

Most businesses sell more than one product. Their product portfolio is the full set. A healthy portfolio has products at different life cycle stages — so that as one declines, a younger one is rising to take its place.

The Boston Matrix (also called the Boston Box) helps a business see this balance. It plots each product against two things: market growth rate on the vertical axis, and market share (relative to the biggest rival) on the horizontal axis. This creates four categories.

Stars — high growth, high share. Fast-growing market and the business is winning it. Needs cash to stay on top, but will become a cash cow later. Electric vehicles for Tesla.

Cash cows — low growth, high share. The market has matured but the business still dominates. Generates steady profits that can fund Stars and Question Marks. Cadbury Dairy Milk chocolate bars.

Question marks — high growth, low share. Fast market but the business has a small slice. Could become a Star with investment, or flop. Risky — needs a decision.

Dogs — low growth, low share. Slow market and the business is losing. Usually withdrawn or sold. Nokia feature phones after the smartphone takeover.

Key Fact

The Boston Matrix axes are market growth rate (vertical) and market share (horizontal). The vertical axis is NOT how fast the product itself is growing — it is how fast the whole market is growing. This is the most common misconception in the exam.

What Do You Do With Each Category?

The Boston Matrix is useful because each category suggests an action. Stars need reinvested cash — the aim is to protect market share as the market grows. Tesla pours money into new Gigafactories to keep its Star position in electric vehicles. Cash Cows are milked — keep them steady with small refreshes, and use the profit to fund riskier products elsewhere. Cadbury Dairy Milk subsidises Mondelez’s newer experimental brands.

Question Marks need a decision: invest heavily to turn them into Stars, or pull the plug. Netflix’s early gaming push was a Question Mark — fast-growing market, low Netflix share — and the firm decided to invest. Dogs are usually withdrawn, sold or quietly wound down because they no longer pay their way. Cadbury discontinued Wispa for seven years in the 1990s when it looked like a Dog, then relaunched it in 2008 after fan campaigns revived demand.

The Boston Matrix has limits too. Drawing it is not a tested exam skill — the focus is on interpretation. And it only uses two axes, so it ignores things like profit margin, brand value and how strategic a product is. A small but iconic product (like Rolls-Royce’s flagship Phantom) might look like a Dog on paper but is crucial for the brand’s image.
before.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to place a product on the Boston Matrix, always explain both axes: is the market growing fast? And does the business have a big share of that market? The top misconception examiners see is confusing market growth with product sales growth — lose this and you lose the point. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, link the category (Star, Cash Cow, Question Mark, Dog) to the action the business should take.

before.content_html:
Why Promote?

Promotion is how a business talks to customers. It is the third of the four Ps. Even a brilliantly designed product at the right price will not sell if nobody knows it exists.

The specification lists four reasons businesses promote: (1) to inform or remind customers about the product, (2) to create or increase sales, (3) to create or change the image of the product, and (4) to persuade customers to buy. A Nike Air Max advert does three or four of these at once — showing the product, building the image, and pushing viewers towards the checkout.

Key Fact

The four reasons for promotion are: inform/remind, create or increase sales, create or change image, and persuade customers to buy. Most adverts aim to do more than one at once.

The Promotional Methods

Advertising covers newspapers, magazines, television, internet and billboards. Cadbury’s Christmas TV adverts have been a UK tradition for years — expensive to make, but they reach millions and build emotional connection. TV reaches mass audiences; internet adverts can be targeted at specific segments; billboards work locally; magazines reach niche readerships.

PR (Public Relations) covers press releases, news stories and community events. It is cheaper than advertising and more credible — a news article carries more weight than a paid advert — but the business cannot control exactly what journalists write.

Sales promotion includes point-of-sale displays, 2-for-1 offers, free gifts, samples, coupons and competitions. Tesco and Boots Meal Deals are a textbook example — customers feel they get extra value and the supermarket shifts more items per visit.

Sponsorship is paying to put a brand on a team, event or show. Emirates sponsoring Arsenal’s stadium and Aviva sponsoring the Premiership Rugby league link these brands with the positive feelings fans have for their sport.

Social media lets brands talk to customers directly through Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and X. Gymshark built a billion-pound brand almost entirely through fitness influencers on Instagram and TikTok — no TV ads needed.

Choosing the Promotional Mix

The promotional mix is the blend of methods a business uses together. Most businesses combine several — Nike runs TV adverts AND sponsors athletes AND pushes Instagram content. Five factors shape the mix:

  • Finance available — TV and Premier League sponsorship are out of reach for a new start-up; social media and local flyers are not.
  • Competitor actions — if rivals are pouring money into TikTok, a business often has to match them to stay visible.
  • Nature of the product or service — complex products (pensions, software) need informative PR and expert reviews; impulse products (chocolate, crisps) suit sales promotions.
  • Nature of the market — consumer markets differ from business-to-business. A bakery promotes to local families; a flour wholesaler promotes through trade magazines.
  • Target market — where does the target customer spend their time? Teenagers are on TikTok; over-60s read newspapers and watch ITV.
Key Fact

The promotional mix is shaped by five factors: finance available, competitor actions, nature of the product/service, nature of the market, and the target market. The right method reaches the right people without wasting budget.

Generic Answers Cap at ~4/6

Examiners are explicit about this: an answer that just describes ‘TV adverts reach lots of people’ without naming a business caps out at about 4 marks on a 6-mark question. Top-band answers name a real UK business, describe their chosen methods, and link each method to their target market. Nike + athlete sponsorship for sports fans. Gymshark + Instagram for Gen Z gym-goers. Cadbury + TV adverts for family audiences at Christmas.

TV advertising reaches mass audiences with strong images and sound, but is very expensive and hard to target precisely. Internet advertising is highly targeted (Google Ads, Meta) and measurable, but viewers use ad-blockers and scroll past. Billboards are cheap per viewer in local areas but cannot carry detailed messages.

PR is cheap and credible but hard to control. Sales promotion drives quick sales but can cheapen the brand if overused — Iceland’s constant half-price offers trained customers to wait for discounts. Sponsorship builds long-term brand image but is slow to pay back. Social media is cheap and two-way, but a bad post can go viral for the wrong reasons — Ratners’ jewellery collapse in the 1990s shows what happens when brand communication goes wrong, even before social media amplified every mistake.

The Mix Has to Match the Stage of the Product

Promotion also shifts across the product life cycle. At launch, promotion is heavy and informative — customers need to know the product exists. During growth, adverts shift to persuasion, showing off the USP. At maturity, reminder adverts keep customers loyal while sales promotions defend against rivals. In decline, promotion is cut back to save cash unless the firm is running an extension strategy.
before.exam_tip_html: For any ‘Analyse’ or ‘Evaluate’ question on promotion, ALWAYS name a real UK business and describe which methods they use. Generic ‘advertising is good because it reaches lots of people’ answers are capped around 4/6. For 9-mark ‘Justify’ questions, explain why your chosen promotional mix beats at least one alternative — e.g. why a new start-up should use TikTok rather than TV adverts.

practice_questions.text:
A business runs a ‘buy one, get one free’ offer in its supermarket for two weeks. Which type of promotion is this?
A) PR
B) Advertising
C) Sales promotion
D) Sponsorship
Give two examples of sales promotion methods listed in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per correct method, up to 2.
Accept any two of: point-of-sale displays, 2-for-1 offers, free gifts, samples, coupons, competitions.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to Gymshark of using social media influencers to promote its clothing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. reaches target market, cheaper than TV, trusted by followers).
2 marks for development (e.g. fitness influencers on Instagram have large followings of gym-goers aged 18–30 — Gymshark’s exact target segment).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so marketing spend reaches the right customers directly and influencer endorsements feel authentic, driving higher conversion than paid TV adverts aimed at a general audience).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business has a £24,000 promotion budget. It spends 30% on social media and the rest on TV adverts. Calculate how much is spent on TV adverts.
practice_questions.marks:
£24,000 × 0.70 = £16,800 (or £24,000 − £7,200).
1 mark for correct method (70% or subtract 30%).
2 marks for correct working.
3 marks for correct final answer of £16,800 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cadbury uses TV advertising at Christmas to increase sales of its chocolate products.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis applied to Cadbury with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. Christmas TV adverts reach mass family audiences watching shows like Strictly → build emotional image linking Cadbury to family and tradition → shoppers buy Dairy Milk tins as gifts → increases December sales and protects Dairy Milk’s Cash Cow position). Answer references image, sales and reach.
Secure (3–4): Two points identified with some application.
Developing (2): One point with limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic generic point with no named business.
[6 marks — generic answers cap around 4]

practice_questions.text: A new independent UK coffee shop is deciding how to promote itself. Justify ONE promotional method they should use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Clear justified decision with sustained reasoning and comparison (e.g. social media — low cost suits a start-up’s small budget, reaches local customers, easy to update with daily specials, beats TV advertising which is unaffordable and too broadly targeted). Includes application to the coffee shop context.
Secure (5–6): Method chosen with reasoning and some comparison.
Developing (3–4): Method chosen with limited justification.
Emerging (1–2): Simple suggestion with no comparison.
[9 marks]

before.content_html:
The Fourth P — Place

Place is the fourth of the four Ps. It covers every route a product takes from factory to customer — shelves, websites, apps, phone orders. The wrong place decision can sink a business: ASOS thrives online because its teen-to-thirties customers shop on their phones. Primark, by contrast, refuses to sell online because impulse-buying in store is central to its model.

Distribution Channels

The AQA specification names three main distribution routes: retailers, wholesalers and telesales.

Retailers are shops that sell directly to the final customer. Tesco, Boots, JD Sports and Primark are retailers. They handle displays, customer service and payments — but take a slice of the final price in return.

Wholesalers sit between producer and retailer. They buy in bulk, break it down, and sell smaller quantities to lots of small shops. A corner-shop owner buys from Booker rather than Coca-Cola direct. Wholesalers cut hassle for both sides but add cost.

Telesales is selling over the phone. Still used by insurance, energy and software sellers, though its share is falling as customers prefer online.

Key Fact

The three distribution channels in the specification are retailers, wholesalers and telesales. A business may use one or several, and the best choice depends on where the target customer actually wants to buy.

E-commerce and M-commerce

E-commerce is buying and selling through websites. M-commerce is the mobile version — apps on phones. ASOS is a UK pioneer: 100% online, no physical shops, reaching customers in over 200 countries. Low overheads mean prices can be competitive, and stock can be updated instantly. The same is true for Ocado in groceries and Zalando in European fashion.

Benefits: reach customers anywhere in the world — ASOS can sell a UK-designed dress in Australia overnight. Low rent and staff costs compared to high-street shops. Open 24/7. Sales data can be tracked and used to refine the product range. Easy to target promotions to segments.

Drawbacks: customers cannot see or try before buying, so returns rates are high — fashion returns can hit 40% and destroy margins. Cyber-security and data protection costs are real. Delivery problems damage the brand. Competition is intense because rivals are only a click away. And traditional strengths like staff expertise (John Lewis) are lost.

E-commerce also opens up international markets. A small Manchester-based soap maker can sell to Japan through its own website or through marketplaces like Amazon, without opening a single overseas shop.

Why the Whole Mix Matters

Each of the four Ps — product, price, promotion, place — matters. But they are not independent. A premium product like an Apple iPhone (product) has a premium price (price), sleek TV adverts (promotion) and is sold in modern Apple Stores or through their online site (place). If Apple suddenly started selling through Poundland, the whole brand image would collapse.

This is the integrated marketing mix. Every element sends the same message to the target customer. Primark: low price, high-street shops, no promotions needed, fashion product. Apple: premium price, flagship stores, slick TV ads, premium product. Consistency is what makes a marketing mix work.

Key Fact

An integrated marketing mix is one where all four Ps — product, price, promotion and place — reinforce the same message to the target customer. Primark and Apple are both examples, even though they target opposite ends of the market.

The Mix Evolves Over Time

The mix is never fixed — customer behaviour, technology and rivals all keep moving. Debenhams failed partly because its mix stopped evolving: same high-street shops, same mid-tier prices, same promotions, while Next invested in e-commerce and ASOS captured the online segment. A business that notices change early — like Domino’s adding the app-ordering ‘place’ channel — wins long-term.

The same logic applies to all four Ps together. Tesco’s marketing mix in 2000 was very different from 2025: the product range has stretched to Finest, Express stores and plant-based ready meals; prices now include Clubcard-only offers; promotion has moved heavily into digital; and place has added online groceries, Tesco Express convenience stores and third-party delivery via Whoosh. Because every element updated together, the mix stayed integrated while each part modernised.

When one P falls out of step with the others, customers get confused and sales suffer. Marks & Spencer spent years with premium-quality clothing (product) and premium prices (price), but promotion and store fit-out felt old-fashioned compared to rivals like Zara and Next — so younger customers never came. M&S had to refresh all four Ps together (modernised stores, refreshed ranges, app-led promotion, new Sparks loyalty scheme) to recover.

Small businesses have the opposite problem. A new Manchester coffee shop may have a brilliant product and great Instagram promotion, but if its place (the shop location) is hidden down a side street, footfall is too low to support the business. All four Ps have to pull their weight.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a pure e-commerce UK retailer?
A) Primark
B) ASOS
C) John Lewis department stores
D) Greggs

practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. selling through mobile phones).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. buying and selling products and services through mobile devices, typically via apps or mobile-optimised websites).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to ASOS of using e-commerce rather than high-street shops.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. reach, 24/7 trading, lower rent, global markets, data collection).
2 marks for development (e.g. ASOS has no high-street rent or shop staff costs, just warehouses and website).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so ASOS’s lower overheads let it offer competitive prices to its fashion-conscious target market while still making a profit, something Debenhams could not match with its expensive shop estate).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A UK fashion retailer sells 60,000 items a month, of which 75% are sold online. Calculate how many items are sold online each month.
practice_questions.marks:
60,000 × 0.75 = 45,000 items.
1 mark for correct method (multiply by 0.75 or 75%).
2 marks for correct working.
3 marks for correct final answer of 45,000 (accept ‘items’).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the four Ps of the marketing mix work together for Primark to create a clear customer message.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis of at least three Ps working together for Primark (e.g. product — fashionable basics; price — low; promotion — almost none, word-of-mouth; place — big flagship stores on main high streets, no online sale). All reinforce the same ‘cheap fast fashion’ image.
Secure (3–4): Two Ps discussed with some application.
Developing (2): One P; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks — generic answers cap around 4]

practice_questions.text: ‘All UK retailers should move fully online to survive.’ Evaluate this statement. Refer to at least one named UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• ASOS and Ocado prove pure online works and reaches global markets.
• Lower overheads — no shop rent, fewer staff.
• Open 24/7; customer data easy to collect for targeted marketing.
• Debenhams’ refusal to move quickly is part of why it collapsed.

Arguments against:
• Primark is hugely profitable without any online sales — its low price depends on impulse in-store buying.
• Some products need physical interaction — John Lewis’s expert service, trying on clothes, perfume testing.
• E-commerce brings high returns costs (40%+ in fashion) that can wipe out margins.
• Cyber-security and delivery issues carry real risk.
• The right answer depends on the product, the target market and the brand image — integrated mix matters more than channel.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with named UK businesses (e.g. ASOS, Primark, John Lewis), clear chains of reasoning and a justified conclusion (e.g. ‘depends on target market and product type’).
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and a conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument on one or both sides; limited application.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points; no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, always link the ‘place’ decision to the target customer — ASOS online for Gen Z, Primark bricks-only for impulse teen shoppers. For 12-mark evaluations, show that you understand the four Ps must work together: a premium product with a cheap distribution channel sends mixed signals. A balanced answer with a named UK business for each side will reach the top band.
